focus: Exodus 10 brings the eighth and ninth plagues, locusts and darkness, as the LORD shows His signs so that Israel will tell its children and grandchildren what He has done. Pharaoh keeps offering terms over who may go and what they may take, confesses sin under pressure, and finally threatens Moses with death, and the chapter ends with Moses announcing that he will never see Pharaoh’s face again.

sections.title: The LORD Warns of Locusts and Gives the Signs a Purpose
sections.summary: The LORD sends Moses to Pharaoh so that Israel may tell “in the hearing of your son and your son’s son” (Exodus 10:2) the signs He has done in Egypt. Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh how long he will refuse to humble himself and warn that locusts will eat everything the hail has left.

sections.title: Pharaoh Offers to Let Only the Men Go
sections.summary: Pharaoh’s servants urge him to let the men go, asking, “Do you not yet know that Egypt is destroyed?” (Exodus 10:7). Moses insists that young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds will go to hold a feast to the LORD, but Pharaoh will allow only the men and drives Moses and Aaron from his presence.

sections.title: Locusts Devour Egypt and Pharaoh Confesses Again
sections.summary: An east wind brings locusts that cover the land and eat every plant and fruit the hail had left. Pharaoh hastily confesses sin and asks forgiveness “only this once” (Exodus 10:17), but after a west wind drives the locusts into the Red Sea, the LORD hardens Pharaoh’s heart.

sections.title: Thick Darkness Covers Egypt While Israel Has Light
sections.summary: Moses stretches out his hand, and darkness “which may even be felt” (Exodus 10:21) covers Egypt for three days, so that no one rises from his place. Yet “all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings” (Exodus 10:23).

sections.title: Pharaoh’s Last Offer and Moses’ Announcement of the Final Break
sections.summary: Pharaoh offers to let the little ones go if the flocks and herds stay behind, but Moses rejects the terms, “not a hoof shall be left behind” (Exodus 10:26), since Israel will learn how to serve the LORD only when they arrive. When the LORD hardens Pharaoh’s heart and Pharaoh threatens Moses with death if he sees his face again, Moses answers, “I will never see your face again” (Exodus 10:29).

1.brief: The LORD sends Moses to Pharaoh and says, “I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his servants,” so that He may show these signs among them. God declares that the hardening of Pharaoh and his court serves His purpose of displaying His signs.
1.explain:
“Now the LORD said to Moses, ‘Go in to Pharaoh;”

The eighth plague begins with another summons. God sends Moses back into the palace even after Pharaoh’s broken promise in 9:34–35.

“for I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his servants, that I may show these signs of Mine before him,”

God tells Moses why He is sending him again. Pharaoh and his officials have hardened themselves (9:34), and God has confirmed them in that course. Their stubbornness will not frustrate God’s plan. It becomes the setting in which He will “show these signs of Mine.”

2.brief: God gives a further purpose: that Israel may tell their sons and grandsons the mighty things He did in Egypt, “that you may know that I am the LORD.” The plagues are meant to be remembered and retold in Israel’s homes for generations.
2.explain:
“and that you may tell in the hearing of your son and your son’s son the mighty things I have done in Egypt,”

God gives a further purpose for the plagues. They are not only for Pharaoh. They are for Israel’s children and grandchildren. Parents are to “tell” what God did, so that the story passes from one generation to the next. The command to teach children reappears in the Passover instructions (12:26–27; 13:8, 14).

“and My signs which I have done among them, that you may know that I am the LORD.”

The goal of the telling is knowledge of God: “that you may know that I am the LORD.” Earlier the plagues were meant to teach Pharaoh and Egypt (7:5, 17; 8:22). Here God says they will also teach Israel, as each generation hears what He did.
2.notes:
The Hebrew verb translated “done” in “the mighty things I have done” can carry the sense of dealing harshly with someone or making sport of them. It pictures God’s complete mastery over Egypt.

Psalm 78:4–5 and Psalm 105:26–36 show Israel doing what this verse commands, retelling the signs in Egypt to later generations.

3.brief: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh in the LORD’s name, “How long will you refuse to humble yourself before Me?” and repeat the demand to let God’s people go. The LORD names pride as the root of Pharaoh’s refusal.
3.explain:
“So Moses and Aaron came in to Pharaoh and said to him, ‘Thus says the LORD God of the Hebrews:”

The brothers deliver God’s message in the familiar form, naming “the LORD God of the Hebrews.”

“How long will you refuse to humble yourself before Me?”

God asks Pharaoh a pointed question about how long he will go on refusing. The issue is not lack of information but pride. Pharaoh has seen enough to know who the LORD is. He will not bow. Pharaoh’s refusal comes from pride, and God calls him to humble himself.

“Let My people go, that they may serve Me.”

The demand remains the same. Humbling himself would mean releasing Israel to serve the LORD.
3.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “humble yourself” means to bow down or be brought low. The same root appears when God says Israel was afflicted (“humbled”) in Egypt (1:11–12). Pharaoh, who afflicted Israel, is now called to be humbled himself.

4.brief: If Pharaoh refuses, the LORD will bring locusts into his territory tomorrow. The eighth plague is announced with a set time.
4.explain:
“Or else, if you refuse to let My people go, behold, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your territory.”

The warning comes with a choice and a set time. If Pharaoh refuses, “tomorrow” the locusts will come. God again announces the plague in advance so its source cannot be mistaken.

5.brief: The locusts will cover the face of the earth and eat whatever the hail left, including every tree in the field. The plague will finish what the hail began.
5.explain:
“And they shall cover the face of the earth, so that no one will be able to see the earth;”

The swarm will be so dense that the ground itself will be hidden. The phrase “the face of the earth” reads literally the eye of the land, as though the land itself could no longer see.

“and they shall eat the residue of what is left, which remains to you from the hail,”

The hail had destroyed the flax and barley but spared the wheat and spelt (9:31–32). The locusts will eat what the hail left. One judgment builds on another.

“and they shall eat every tree which grows up for you out of the field.”

Even the trees will be stripped. Egypt’s remaining food supply is about to disappear.
5.notes: Locust swarms were a known disaster in the ancient Near East and still occur in the region today. A large swarm can strip crops and leaves over a wide area in a short time. Joel 1–2 describes such a plague in Judah.

6.brief: The locusts will fill the houses of Pharaoh, his servants, and all Egypt, in numbers never seen before, and Moses turns and leaves Pharaoh. Moses delivers the warning and walks out without waiting for a reply.
6.explain:
“They shall fill your houses, the houses of all your servants, and the houses of all the Egyptians—”

The locusts will not stay in the fields. They will enter homes at every level of society, from Pharaoh’s palace to ordinary houses.

“which neither your fathers nor your fathers’ fathers have seen, since the day that they were on the earth to this day.”

The plague will be unlike anything in Egypt’s memory. No generation has seen its equal.

“And he turned and went out from Pharaoh.”

Moses delivers the warning and leaves without waiting for an answer. His departure leaves the decision with Pharaoh.

7.brief: Pharaoh’s servants ask, “How long shall this man be a snare to us?” and urge him to let the men go, asking, “Do you not yet know that Egypt is destroyed?” Pharaoh’s own officials now see that Egypt is ruined and press him to yield.
7.explain:
“Then Pharaoh’s servants said to him, ‘How long shall this man be a snare to us?”

For the first time Pharaoh’s own officials press him to yield. They use the same words “How long” that God used in 10:3. They call Moses “a snare,” a trap that keeps catching them. They see that resisting is ruining them.

“Let the men go, that they may serve the LORD their God.”

The officials propose a compromise. “Let the men go.” They may mean only the men, or they may simply be urging Pharaoh to release the people. Either way, they want Pharaoh to give in before worse comes.

“Do you not yet know that Egypt is destroyed?”

The officials see what Pharaoh refuses to admit. “Egypt is destroyed.” The country’s crops, livestock, and health have been struck. The king’s own advisors now recognize the ruin his stubbornness has brought.
7.notes: Some of Pharaoh’s servants had already feared the word of the LORD before the hail (9:20). Their counsel here shows the pressure growing within Pharaoh’s own court.

8.brief: Moses and Aaron are brought back to Pharaoh, who tells them to go and serve the LORD but asks, “Who are the ones that are going?” Pharaoh appears to give way but begins to set limits.
8.explain:
“So Moses and Aaron were brought again to Pharaoh, and he said to them, ‘Go, serve the LORD your God.”

Moses and Aaron are brought back, and Pharaoh seems to give way. “Go, serve the LORD your God.”

“Who are the ones that are going?”

Then he adds a condition by asking who will go. Pharaoh wants to control who leaves. His apparent permission is about to become a negotiation.

9.brief: Moses answers that all will go, young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds, “for we must hold a feast to the LORD.” The whole people, with their children and animals, belong at the feast God has called them to.
9.explain:
“And Moses said, ‘We will go with our young and our old; with our sons and our daughters,”

Moses answers without compromise. Everyone will go: “our young and our old,” “our sons and our daughters.” No part of the people will be left behind.

“with our flocks and our herds we will go, for we must hold a feast to the LORD.”

The animals will go too. The reason is worship: “we must hold a feast to the LORD.” A feast was a celebration for the whole community, including families. Moses insists that the whole people belongs at the feast God has called.
9.notes: The Hebrew word translated “feast” refers to a pilgrimage festival, a sacred gathering in which the whole community took part. Israel’s later feasts included sons, daughters, servants, and others in the household (Deuteronomy 16:11, 14).

10.brief: Pharaoh mockingly says the LORD had better be with them if he lets them and their little ones go, and warns, “Beware, for evil is ahead of you.” He treats the request for the children as proof of bad intentions.
10.explain:
“Then he said to them, ‘The LORD had better be with you when I let you and your little ones go!”

Pharaoh answers with sarcasm. “The LORD had better be with you” if he ever lets them and their children go. He means that he will never allow it. The words mock the LORD and the request.

“Beware, for evil is ahead of you.”

Pharaoh adds a warning. “Evil is ahead of you.” He may mean that Israel has evil intentions, planning to escape for good. He may also be threatening them. Either way, he treats the request for the children as proof that Israel is not planning to return.
10.notes: The phrase translated “evil is ahead of you” reads literally evil is before your faces. Some interpreters see a play on the name of the Egyptian sun god Ra, whose name sounds like the Hebrew word for evil. The suggestion is possible but uncertain.

11.brief: Pharaoh refuses and says only the men may go and serve the LORD, and Moses and Aaron are driven out from his presence. He offers a partial release that would keep the families behind in Egypt.
11.explain:
“Not so! Go now, you who are men, and serve the LORD, for that is what you desired.”

Pharaoh refuses the full request. “Not so!” Only “you who are men” may go. He claims this is what they asked for, though Moses had said everyone would go. Keeping the women and children in Egypt would ensure the men came back. Pharaoh offers only a partial release that keeps the families in his hands.

“And they were driven out from Pharaoh’s presence.”

The meeting ends with Moses and Aaron thrown out. Pharaoh will not hear more.

12.brief: The LORD tells Moses to stretch out his hand over Egypt so that locusts come and eat every plant the hail has left. God carries out His warning after Pharaoh’s refusal.
12.explain:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts,”

God responds to Pharaoh’s refusal. Moses is to stretch out his hand, and the locusts will come as announced.

“that they may come upon the land of Egypt, and eat every herb of the land—all that the hail has left.”

The purpose is to consume “all that the hail has left.” God carries out exactly what He warned in 10:5.

13.brief: Moses stretches out his rod, and the LORD brings an east wind all day and night, which carries the locusts by morning. The LORD controls the wind that brings the plague.
13.explain:
“So Moses stretched out his rod over the land of Egypt,”

Moses obeys and raises the rod.

“and the LORD brought an east wind on the land all that day and all that night.”

“The LORD brought an east wind.” The wind blows for a full day and night. God uses a natural means, but He directs it. The timing, direction, and result are all His.

“When it was morning, the east wind brought the locusts.”

By morning the wind has carried the swarm into Egypt. The plague arrives just as God said.
13.notes: An east wind would blow from the Arabian desert. The same wind appears again at the Red Sea, where God uses a strong east wind to divide the waters (14:21).

14.brief: The locusts cover all Egypt and settle on its whole territory, more severe than any before or after. The plague is unprecedented, as God said.
14.explain:
“And the locusts went up over all the land of Egypt and rested on all the territory of Egypt.”

The swarm covers the whole country and settles on every part of it.

“They were very severe; previously there had been no such locusts as they, nor shall there be such after them.”

The plague is unique, as God had warned (10:6). No locust swarm before or after compares with it in Egypt.
14.notes: Joel 2:2 uses similar language of the locust army in his day. Each statement describes an unmatched disaster in its own setting.

15.brief: The locusts cover the ground until the land is darkened and eat every plant of the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left, so that nothing green remains in Egypt. The vegetation the hail spared is now gone as well.
15.explain:
“For they covered the face of the whole earth, so that the land was darkened;”

The swarm was so thick that “the land was darkened.” This darkness anticipates the next plague, when darkness will cover Egypt completely (10:21–23).

“and they ate every herb of the land and all the fruit of the trees which the hail had left.”

Everything the hail spared is now eaten. The wheat and spelt (9:32) are gone.

“So there remained nothing green on the trees or on the plants of the field throughout all the land of Egypt.”

The verse sums up the devastation. “Nothing green” remained. Egypt’s fields and orchards are bare.

16.brief: Pharaoh calls Moses and Aaron in haste and says, “I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you.” Under the pressure of the plague, Pharaoh confesses again.
16.explain:
“Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron in haste,”

Pharaoh acts “in haste.” The man who just drove Moses out now calls him back in a hurry.

“and said, ‘I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you.”

For the second time Pharaoh confesses sin (9:27). This time he adds that he has sinned “against you,” against Moses and Aaron as well. Under the pressure of the plague, Pharaoh again confesses.

17.brief: Pharaoh asks them to forgive his sin “only this once” and to entreat the LORD to take away “this death only.” His request focuses on removing the plague rather than on obeying God.
17.explain:
“Now therefore, please forgive my sin only this once,”

Pharaoh asks for forgiveness “only this once.” The phrase reveals how he thinks. He treats his sin as a single lapse, not a settled pattern of rebellion. He has made and broken such promises before (8:8, 15, 28, 32; 9:28, 34).

“and entreat the LORD your God, that He may take away from me this death only.”

His real concern appears in the request. He wants God to “take away from me this death only.” He calls the plague “this death,” a deadly disaster. Pharaoh’s request focuses on removing the plague rather than on obeying God.

18.brief: Moses goes out from Pharaoh and entreats the LORD. Moses again intercedes for the king.
18.explain:
“So he went out from Pharaoh and entreated the LORD.”

Moses goes out and prays for Pharaoh again. Moses again intercedes for the king, even though Pharaoh has broken his word before.

19.brief: The LORD turns a very strong west wind that carries the locusts into the Red Sea, so that not one remains in Egypt. The LORD removes the plague as completely as He sent it.
19.explain:
“And the LORD turned a very strong west wind, which took the locusts away and blew them into the Red Sea.”

God reverses the wind. “A very strong west wind” carries the locusts away. The wind that brought them from the east now sweeps them out to the sea.

“There remained not one locust in all the territory of Egypt.”

The removal is complete. “Not one locust” remained. The LORD removes the plague as completely as He sent it.
19.notes:
The phrase translated “west wind” reads literally “sea wind,” a wind from the Mediterranean.

The Hebrew name for the “Red Sea” is “Yam Suph,” which can mean Sea of Reeds. Scholars debate the exact body of water meant here and at the crossing (13:18; 15:4). The name is used in the Old Testament for the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba as well.

20.brief: “But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart,” and he did not let Israel go. God’s announced hardening continues, and Pharaoh still refuses.
20.explain:
“But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let the children of Israel go.”

Once again the plague is removed, and once again Pharaoh refuses. “The LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart.” God confirms Pharaoh in the stubbornness he has chosen, as announced in 10:1.

21.brief: The LORD tells Moses to stretch out his hand toward heaven so that darkness will cover Egypt, “darkness which may even be felt.” The ninth plague comes without warning and is described as darkness thick enough to feel.
21.explain:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt,”

The ninth plague, like the third and sixth, comes without warning. Moses is to stretch out his hand “toward heaven,” and darkness will fall over Egypt.

“darkness which may even be felt.”

The darkness will be so thick that it “may even be felt.” This is not an ordinary night. It is a darkness heavy enough to seem tangible.
21.notes:
The sun god was among Egypt’s most important deities, and Pharaoh was regarded as the son of the sun god Ra. A plague of darkness would show the LORD’s power over the source of light that Egypt worshiped. The text itself does not name the sun god, so this connection is drawn from Egypt’s background.

Some interpreters connect the darkness with a severe sandstorm (the khamsin) known in Egypt. The text presents it as the direct act of God.

22.brief: Moses stretches out his hand, and there is thick darkness in all Egypt for three days. The land that refused the LORD is plunged into darkness.
22.explain:
“So Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days.”

The darkness falls for “three days.” It covers “all the land of Egypt.” The land that refused the LORD is plunged into darkness.
22.notes: The Hebrew word translated “thick darkness” is the word for gloom or deep darkness, also used for the darkness of the Day of the LORD (Joel 2:2; Zephaniah 1:15).

23.brief: The Egyptians cannot see one another or move from their places for three days, “But all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings.” God’s distinction between His people and Egypt is now as plain as light and darkness.
23.explain:
“They did not see one another; nor did anyone rise from his place for three days.”

The darkness paralyzed Egypt. People could not see each other and did not move from where they were for three days. All work and movement stopped.

“But all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings.”

The contrast is striking. Every Israelite home had light. God’s distinction between His people and Egypt is now as plain as light and darkness. The text does not explain how the light came. It simply records that God’s people had light while Egypt sat in darkness.

24.brief: Pharaoh calls Moses and offers to let the people and their little ones go if the flocks and herds stay behind. Pharaoh offers new terms that would keep Israel’s animals in Egypt.
24.explain:
“Then Pharaoh called to Moses and said, ‘Go, serve the LORD;”

Pharaoh calls Moses again. “Go, serve the LORD.” He seems to yield further.

“only let your flocks and your herds be kept back. Let your little ones also go with you.”

Now he will allow the children to go, but “only” if the animals stay. This is Pharaoh’s fourth attempt at compromise (8:25, 28; 10:11). By holding the livestock, he would keep Israel’s wealth and the means of their worship, and he would ensure they came back.

25.brief: Moses answers that Pharaoh must also give them sacrifices and burnt offerings to offer to the LORD their God. Worship requires the animals Pharaoh wants to keep.
25.explain:
“But Moses said, ‘You must also give us sacrifices and burnt offerings, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.”

Moses not only refuses the condition but adds to the demand. “You must also give us sacrifices and burnt offerings.” Pharaoh will not only let the animals go. He will contribute animals for the sacrifices. Worship requires the animals Pharaoh wants to keep.
25.notes: The Hebrew word for “burnt offerings” describes an offering that goes up, wholly burned on the altar. Leviticus 1 later gives the law for this offering.

26.brief: Moses insists, “not a hoof shall be left behind,” because they do not know what they must offer to the LORD until they arrive. God alone will tell them what He requires, so Israel cannot leave anything behind.
26.explain:
“Our livestock also shall go with us; not a hoof shall be left behind.”

Moses insists on complete release. “Not a hoof shall be left behind.” Not one animal, not even one hoof, will remain in Egypt.

“For we must take some of them to serve the LORD our God,”

The reason is worship. The animals are needed to “serve the LORD.” Leaving them behind would hinder Israel from obeying God.

“and even we do not know with what we must serve the LORD until we arrive there.”

Moses adds that even Israel does not yet know what God will require. God alone sets the terms of worship. Israel must bring everything, because God will tell them what He requires when they arrive.

27.brief: “But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not let them go.” The final offer ends in refusal, as God has been saying all along.
27.explain:
“But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not let them go.”

Pharaoh refuses again. “The LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart.” The final offer ends in refusal, as God has said all along.

28.brief: Pharaoh orders Moses to get away and warns him never to see his face again, “For in the day you see my face you shall die!” Pharaoh threatens Moses with death and orders him out, and Moses answers in the next verse.
28.explain:
“Then Pharaoh said to him, ‘Get away from me! Take heed to yourself and see my face no more!”

Pharaoh explodes in anger. “Get away from me!” He orders Moses never to appear before him again.

“For in the day you see my face you shall die!”

Pharaoh threatens Moses with death. The king has gone from negotiation to open hostility.

29.brief: Moses answers, “You have spoken well. I will never see your face again.” Moses announces the final break, though the same audience continues in Exodus 11:4–8 before he leaves.
29.explain:
“So Moses said, ‘You have spoken well. I will never see your face again.”

Moses accepts Pharaoh’s words. “You have spoken well.” He agrees that he will “never see your face again.” In Moses’ words the break is final. The natural reading is that this same audience continues in 11:4–8, where Moses announces the last plague. That continuation is an inference from the flow of the text. What the text states outright is that Moses then went out from Pharaoh in great anger (11:8), and that Pharaoh later summoned Moses and Aaron by night (12:31).
29.notes: Exodus 11:1–3 records what God had told Moses. It stands between Moses’ words in 10:29 and his announcement to Pharaoh in 11:4–8.
